articles.author: Ahmed Allam
articles.description:
When an AI agent makes a decision, it evaluates several options and picks one. The rest disappear forever — you never see what it almost did or why it rejected the alternatives.
I built GhostTrace to fix that.
It captures "Phantom Branches": the actions your agent considered but rejected, with the full reasoning for each rejection. Everything is saved to a .ghost.json file that you can replay and inspect anytime.
ghosttrace record

✓ Recorded 4 decisions with 5 phantom branches
📄 Saved to gt_a1b2c3d4.ghost.json

ghosttrace replay gt_ghost.json --show-phantoms

Step 1: ✓ read_file → src/auth.py
👻 REJECTED: write_file (premature)
👻 REJECTED: search_codebase (too broad)

Super simple to get started:
pip install ghosttrace

GitHub: https://github.com/AhmedAllam0/ghosttrace

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/ghosttrace/



It's framework-agnostic for now, but what should I integrate first?

LangChain? CrewAI? OpenAI Agents SDK?  
Feedback very welcome — let me know what you think, if you'll try it, or what features you'd love to see! 🔥




![ ](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/nvd4317vowb62srn3hqx.png)
articles.title: GhostTrace: Capture "Phantom Branches" to Debug Rejected Decisions in AI Agents

how the model is being set up to think and respond.

articles.author: MaxxMini
articles.description:
Last week, I launched 27 browser games on itch.io. In one batch. Here's what went wrong — and the lessons that actually stuck.
I published games with zero screenshots. Just a title and a "Run Game" button. Turns out, people don't click things that look abandoned.
Fix: Even a single gameplay screenshot increases click-through dramatically. I went back and added screenshots to my top 5 games — those are now the only ones getting any traffic.
itch.io's discovery system relies heavily on tags. I launched with generic tags like "game" and "browser." That's like tagging your npm package "code."
Fix: Research what tags successful games in your genre use. For my puzzle games, puzzle, casual, short, singleplayer performed way better than generic labels.
27 games sounds impressive. But most were min…
